q7.answer: The client does not copy the key when it is built. On every provider call it asks the in-memory secret holder for the current key, so a refresh swap (done per key, atomically, every 5 minutes plus jitter) reaches the next call. A new version therefore takes effect within about 5 minutes without a restart.

q8.answer: By a check-only step after the rollout completes: all 4 pods must run the new image digest, and each pod's logs must show the version ids recorded when the keys were written, for all three keys, over a log window covering at least one full refresh cycle after the last pod was replaced. If a newer version id exists, the check repeats against it. Any failure stops the process and nothing is revoked. Whether an internal endpoint should expose version ids to speed this up is still an open question (open question 7), so the log-based check is the decided method.

q9.answer: The intended order is: (1) confirm provider overlap; (2) set store entries, KMS keys and access rules; (3) create new keys at each provider and test them while the old keys stay active; (4) write the new values to the store; (5) merge one pull request that switches the app to read from the store and removes the api_keys from config/app.yaml, then roll out to staging and prod; (6) confirm every instance is on the new keys; (7) revoke the old keys at the providers; (8) clean up the repo and logs. The plan ships the store switch and the config removal in the same pull request, so it does not sequence those two separately.

q10.answer: make run reads the same non-secret config/app.yaml, then reads orders-api/dev/* using the developer's dev-only identity through the same loader as production, holding the values in memory only. The keys are provider sandbox keys or the team's agreed test keys, never live keys, and the developer identity has no read access to orders-api/prod/*. If the developer has no dev access, the process refuses to start, and the documented opt-in fallback is a provider sandbox or local stub.

q11.answer: The plan treats it as a startup failure: the instance does not become ready, retries under the same budget (one attempt plus 3 retries, about 6 seconds), logs the failure without any secret values, and exits non-zero so the rollout halts while old pods keep serving. This was written as the intended behaviour but is flagged as open question 5, which still needs confirmation from the team.
